text: Harrow Creek Goods runs a two-service order-processing app: an api service that accepts requests and writes jobs to a queue, and a worker that drains that queue and does the slow work. This lab takes that app from running on a laptop to running on the cluster, using nothing but the Docker and Kubernetes fundamentals from the first three chapters.

Both services share one codebase, so a single multi-stage Dockerfile builds both images. The build stage installs dependencies once; the runtime stage copies only the built app directory into a distroless base and drops to a non-root user. A build arg called ENTRYPOINT_FILE picks api.js or worker.js at build time, which is what lets one Dockerfile produce two different images.

Each image gets built and tagged separately, with a real version -- 1.0.0, not latest -- then pushed to the registry. That choice isn't cosmetic: if every deploy overwrote the same latest tag, there would be no previous image left to roll back to when something goes wrong.

The api service gets a Deployment with three replicas and a Service in front of it, because other things need to call it over the network. The worker gets a Deployment too, but no Service at all -- nothing ever addresses the worker directly, it only pulls from a queue, so giving it a Service would just be an unused object sitting in the cluster.

After kubectl apply on both manifests, the real verification isn't the absence of an error message. It's kubectl get pods showing every replica Running with READY at 1/1, and kubectl get endpoints order-api showing a real endpoint behind the Service for each ready pod -- proof the Service's selector actually found the Deployment's pods.

With both services deployed and verified, Lesson 30 builds on top of this exact app: adding Ingress to route external traffic in, a PersistentVolumeClaim for data that needs to survive a pod restart, and wrapping the whole thing in a Helm chart instead of hand-applied YAML.
